c1.title: ZhiftCRM Consultant — Platform & Dashboard Command
c1.desc: The platform as a consultant supports it: access and the two records behind one person, the dashboard's three bands, the status wall and how to read it as a shape, the timeframe that rules the page, and what the three charts answer that the cards cannot.

lessons.title: Access, credentials, and sessions — what you'll support daily
lessons.html:
Half of week-one tickets are access, and none of them are interesting. Know the shape cold so you can clear them in a sentence.

What a person needs to log in: an account created by an administrator, the tenant URL, and a modern browser. Nothing else. There is no self-registration — if somebody has no account, an administrator creates one, and that is the whole answer to "how do I sign up".

The tenant URL is per client. Sessions belong to a browser and a tenant. A consultant working three clients in one browser will be logged into one of them, and the symptom is data that looks wrong rather than an error message. Use separate profiles or a private window per tenant and you remove a whole category of confusion — including your own.

The two failures that look identical and are not. "I can log in but the page is empty" is almost always scope: the account exists, has no reporting tier or no assigned records, and is correctly showing nothing. "I cannot log in" is credentials. Establish which you are looking at before touching anything, because the fixes are in different places and one of them is not yours.

The account and the person are different objects. A User is who logs in. A Closer is the sales record that leads attach to, and it links to a User. Creating one does not create the other, and the commonest onboarding fault in the whole product is a closer who exists as a person, exists as a User, and has no Closer record — so auto-assignment never sees them and they sit idle wondering why no leads arrive. That is chapter one of module five, and it starts here.

DRILL: A new starter says the dashboard is blank on day one. Two questions, in order? — Can they see anything at all, or is the page empty? Empty means scope, so check their tier and whether a Closer record exists. If they cannot reach a page at all, it is credentials or the wrong tenant URL. Do not begin with the data.

Why access tickets are worth answering well rather than fast. They are a client's first experience of your support, they arrive in the first week when confidence is being formed, and they are the only tickets where the answer is always knowable. A consultant who is crisp here buys a great deal of patience for the harder questions later.

The session trap in a training session. Running a workshop from one browser, demonstrating as an administrator, then telling closers "your screen will look like this" — it will not. Administrators see everything; closers see their own. Demonstrate from a closer's login when teaching closers, or you will train them on a screen they never get.

lessons.title: The dashboard — layout, hierarchy, and role-based views
lessons.html:
The dashboard answers "where is work piling up" in seconds, and it is built in three bands, top to bottom.

Band one: the timeframe. A caption states the current scope in words — Showing this month — with the selector at the right: Day · Week · Month · Quarter · Year. Everything below obeys it. Read the caption before reading any number; it is the single commonest cause of a client and a consultant looking at different figures on the same screen.

Band two: the status cards. Around two dozen of them, each a label and a number, laid out in rows. They fall into two groups sitting side by side — lifecycle cards describing where orders are in the flow, and performance cards describing outcomes and rates for the period. Most are live counts; some are percentages, such as Delivery Rate (Period).

Every card is a shortcut. Click one and the Orders list opens filtered to exactly the orders behind that number. For a closer the list narrows to their own. This is the fastest route in the product from "there are 45 on hold" to the specific list to work, and clients routinely never discover it.

The set of cards is not fixed. It is driven by the system and the selected timeframe, so the row can change as the business configuration changes. That is intentional — the dashboard surfaces the buckets that matter rather than a permanent list. Teach it as a live surface, not a layout to memorise.

Band three: three charts. Delivered Value Trend (revenue progression), Outcome Breakdown (operational outcomes), and Status Distribution (share by status). The next chapters take the cards and the charts in turn.

DRILL: A client says the dashboard "changed overnight — cards have moved". Is this a fault? — Almost certainly not. The card set follows system configuration and the selected timeframe. Check what changed in configuration before raising anything, and reassure them the surface is meant to move.

Why the caption matters more than the selector. The selector shows a highlighted button; the caption says Showing this month in plain words. In a call, ask the client to read you the caption rather than describe the buttons. It removes an entire class of misunderstanding in one sentence.

The card that teaches the product. AGENT UPDATE holds orders just updated by delivery agents, so closers can see current agent activity without hunting. It exists because closers were chasing agents for information the system already had. When a client asks what a card is for rather than what it counts, that is the shape of the answer.

lessons.title: KPI cards — every formula, and reading them as a set
lessons.html:
There is no single "revenue" card. The dashboard is a wall of order counts by status, plus a few rates, and reading it means reading the shape rather than any one number.

The lifecycle cards follow an order through its life: Total Orders, Agent Update, Assigned, Agent Notified, Dispatch Assigned, Order Accepted, Delivery In Progress, Delivery Rescheduled, and onward to the outcomes — Delivered, Cancelled, Rejected, Duplicate, No Stock, Failed / Returned, Not Reachable, Not Picking, Call Back, Not Ready, On Hold.

The period cards are a different animal and get misread constantly: Assigned (Period) · Rescheduled (Today) · Rescheduled (Tomorrow) · Rejected (Period) · Delivery Rate (Period). A card without "(Period)" and one with it are answering different questions, and a client comparing them will find a discrepancy that is not one.

Delivery Rate (Period) is the only ratio in the wall: delivered against total, as a percentage. Everything else is a count. A rate and a count do not move together — a good month can raise the count and lower the rate, and that is the most useful sentence you can teach a client about this screen.

Read them as a set, in three moves. First, a big number in an early-stage bucket means leads are waiting and nobody is working them. Second, a build-up in a mid-stage bucket points at delivery or fulfilment rather than at closers. Third, when a number surprises you, click through immediately — the list behind the count almost always explains it faster than reasoning about it does.

DRILL: Not Ready shows 37,839 while Delivered shows 12 for the same month. Is the business failing? — No: those two cards are not scoped alike. Delivered is counting the period; the large lifecycle counts are standing populations that accumulate. Click both before concluding anything — the shape of the wall is a map, not a scoreboard.

Why "scan at the start of each shift" is the actual instruction. The cards reward a habit, not an analysis. Thirty seconds at the top of a shift tells a closer where the work is; the same wall studied for twenty minutes tells them very little more. Teach the habit and the click-through, and leave the deep reads to the reports.

The trap in teaching formulas here. Consultants like formulas because they are teachable. Most of these cards are counts of a status, so the formula is the status definition — which means module two, on the order lifecycle, is where the real teaching happens. Explaining a card without knowing what its status means operationally is how a consultant sounds fluent and helps nobody.

lessons.title: Timeframes — the filter that rules the page
lessons.html:
One control, top right, five options: Day · Week · Month · Quarter · Year. It drives the cards and the charts together, and a caption beneath the page title states the result in words — Showing this month.

It is the first thing to check and almost the last thing anyone checks. Nearly every "these numbers are wrong" conversation ends here. Two people on a call looking at the same dashboard on different timeframes will disagree indefinitely and neither will be wrong.

The timeframe is not the same control as a report's date filter. Reports carry their own — Daily, Monthly, Custom with from and to — and several carry a Date Type field deciding which date is filtered, such as Order Date. The dashboard has no Date Type: it is a live operational surface, not an analysis tool. Expecting it to reconcile to a report on a chosen date basis is a category error, and worth saying out loud before a client tries it.

What each window is actually good for. Day is the shift view — what arrived and what is stuck right now. Week is the coordination view, long enough to absorb a bad Tuesday. Month is the management view and the default for most conversations. Quarter and Year exist for trend, and are the wrong lens for operational decisions, because a fortnight of trouble disappears inside a quarter.

DRILL: A client insists delivery rate has collapsed; your screen shows it healthy. Neither of you has changed anything. First move? — Ask them to read the caption aloud. If they are on Day and you are on Month, you are both looking at the truth and at different truths. Agree the window before agreeing anything else.

Why the operational default should be Month, and the operational habit should be Day. Month is where targets, budgets and conversations live, so it is the right default for a screen a manager opens. Day is where work is, so it is the right habit for a closer at the start of a shift. A client who sets one default for everybody has made one of those two groups worse off.

The reconciliation conversation, had once and early. Dashboard and reports will differ. The dashboard is live and scoped by a simple window; reports carry date type, brand, branch, country and tier scope. Put that in writing at handover and you will not have the same call every month.

checks.q: Quarter and Year are the wrong lens for operational decisions because:
opts: A fortnight of trouble disappears inside them
checks.why: Trend windows smooth away exactly the signal an operational decision needs.

lessons.title: The charts — reading, interaction, cross-reads
lessons.html:
Three charts sit below the cards, and each answers a different question.

Delivered Value Trend — subtitled revenue progression. Value delivered over the selected window, plotted as a line with the area beneath it filled. It answers "is money actually landing", and it moves only when orders reach Delivered. A flat line with busy cards above it means plenty of activity and nothing completing.

Outcome Breakdown — subtitled operational outcomes. A bar chart comparing how orders ended. It answers "when orders finish, how do they finish", which is the question the status wall cannot answer because counts sitting in mid-flight drown it.

Status Distribution — subtitled share by status. A doughnut giving proportion rather than count. It answers "what does the book look like", and it is the chart to show a client who is anxious about one large number: a frightening count is often an unremarkable share.

The cross-read that matters. Take Delivered Value Trend against Outcome Breakdown. Rising value with a healthy outcome mix is a good month. Rising value with a worsening mix means volume is covering a quality problem, and it will stop covering it. Neither chart shows that alone; the pair does, and pointing it out is the sort of thing clients remember a consultant for.

What the charts are not. They are a live operational read on the selected window, not analysis. Cohorts, attribution, product mix and return on ad spend all live in Reports, and a client trying to run strategy off the dashboard charts is using a thermometer to plan a holiday.

DRILL: Delivered Value Trend is flat for three weeks then spikes at the end. The client is delighted. What do you check? — Whether orders were completing all along or whether a batch was marked delivered in one go. A spike at a period end is often an administrative event rather than a commercial one, and the Outcome Breakdown beside it usually says which.

Why proportion calms people and counts alarm them. A client seeing 37,839 in a bucket reacts to the digits. The same figure as a slice of a doughnut is a shape they can judge. When a conversation is heated, move it to Status Distribution — not to soften the news, but because share is the honest frame for "is this normal".

The habit worth installing. Cards to find where work is stuck; charts to find whether the month is behaving; reports for anything that requires a decision about money. Three surfaces, three jobs. Clients who conflate them end up making budget decisions off a live counter.

c2.title: ZhiftCRM Consultant — Orders, Customers & Fulfilment
c2.desc: Orders end to end at consultant level: the list and why filters explain most missing orders, order creation with the duplicate and consolidation settings you configure, the status spine and the four terminal statuses that drive the follow-up pool, the drawer, editing money safely, assignment and after-sales, and the customer directory as the other axis on the same data.

lessons.title: The orders list — search, filters, and who sees what
lessons.html:
Orders is the operational heart, and visibility is scoped from the first pixel: closers see their own, managers see everything. Teach that before any conversation about missing orders, because "I can't find it" is usually scope rather than search.

The columns, and what each is for: Order (customer name with phone beneath) · Created · Status · Category · Closer · Branch · Brand · Value · Delivery · Last Updated · Call. Two carry more than they appear to — Category shows the product with its source beneath it, so you can see at a glance whether an order came from a campaign form or arrived online; and Brand can hold more than one.

The top bar is three controls and two buttons: a search across customer, phone and order; a status filter; a closer filter; then Create Order, More filters and Reset. Reset exists because the filters persist, and a client convinced that orders have disappeared has very often left a filter on from yesterday. Check Reset before you check anything else.

More filters opens the advanced set, and it is where real diagnosis happens: Channel · Assigned Agent · Digital Marketer · Country · Brand · Category · Branch · Date Type · From Date · To Date. Date Type is the one to point out — it decides which date the range applies to, so the same range answers a different question depending on what is selected.

The scale changes how you teach it. A working installation runs to hundreds of thousands of orders across thousands of pages. Nobody browses this list. The competent motion is filter first, then read — and the fastest route in is usually not this screen at all but a dashboard card, which opens the list already filtered to exactly the orders behind that number.

DRILL: A manager says half their orders vanished this morning. First three checks? — Reset the filters; confirm the date range and Date Type; then confirm their scope. Data loss is the last hypothesis, not the first, and in practice it is the first check about nine times in ten.

Why Date Type deserves a sentence in every handover. A client reconciling "August orders" against "August deliveries" will get two different numbers and conclude something is broken. They are filtering the same range on different dates. Said once at handover, it never becomes a ticket; discovered by a finance manager at month end, it becomes an escalation.

The Call button is a design statement. It sits on the row, not behind the order, because the intended motion is to work the list rather than to study it. When a client asks why there is no bulk-edit, that is the answer: this screen is for acting on one order at a time, quickly.

lessons.title: Creating an order — every field, and the duplicate check
lessons.html:
Create Order sits top-right of the Orders list. The dialog is unremarkable until the duplicate check fires, which is the part worth teaching.

The fields, with the traps. Customer name searches existing customers as you type — selecting a match pulls in their details rather than creating a second customer record, and skipping past the match is how duplicate customers are born. Phone is the identity field in practice, because it is what the duplicate check uses. Address, category, items, quantity and value follow; brand and cost centre derive from the category rather than being chosen.

The duplicate check is configurable, and a consultant sets it. Four settings govern it. Enable Duplicate Check is the master switch and covers both the public form and manual order paths. Duplicate Check Window (days) decides how far back to look — and zero disables the window entirely. Require Matching Items, when on, means duplicates must share the same set of item codes; turn it off to flag any prior order from the same phone regardless of what was ordered. Run on Manual Orders gives closers a duplicate-warning banner while creating an order, and they can override and proceed.

That override is deliberate and worth defending to a client. A customer genuinely may order twice in a day. A hard block would turn a warning into lost revenue and teach closers to work around the system. The banner informs; the human decides.

Open-Order Consolidation is the neighbouring behaviour and gets confused with duplication. When on, a new online order from a customer who already has an open, not-yet-dispatched order in the same city and state is merged into that existing order rather than creating a second — one delivery, one fee. It is off by default. The consolidation window is short by design: one day means the same calendar day, and widening it increases the chance of merging genuinely different addresses.

DRILL: A client wants duplicate warnings to become a hard block because closers ignore them. Your answer? — The override exists because legitimate repeat orders exist. If closers are overriding routinely, the window or the matching rule is wrong, not the override. Tighten the configuration and look at why the warning is firing so often.

Duplication and consolidation solve opposite halves of one problem. The duplicate check stops you recording the same order twice. Consolidation stops you delivering twice to somebody who ordered twice legitimately. A client who turns on one and expects the other's behaviour will report a fault that is a misunderstanding.

Why Restrict Order Merge to Same Brand is off by default. Cross-brand merges within the same business and currency are allowed, because the saving is the delivery fee and brands often operate together. Turn it on only where brands run as independent units that should never share a delivery — and know that doing so costs the client that saving.

lessons.title: The statuses — lifecycle, owners, and what counts as finished
lessons.html:
Status drives visibility, responsibility, every KPI and the automations behind them. There are more of them than people expect — the cluster report alone carries seventeen columns — so learn the shape rather than the list.

The spine, in order: New Lead → Qualified → Confirmed → Assigned → Agent Notified → Dispatch Assigned → Order Accepted → Processing → Delivery In Progress → Delivered.

The departures from it, each meaning something different: Delivery Rescheduled · On Hold · Not Ready · Call Back · Not Picking · Not Reachable · No Stock · Failed / Returned · Rejected · Cancelled · Duplicate · Delivered Order Cancelled.

Four statuses are terminal, and the product names them: Delivered, Cancelled, Duplicate, Rescheduled. This is not trivia — it is the rule the follow-up pool uses. Orders not in a terminal status automatically enter the pool after a configured number of days from creation. Everything else keeps being chased.

Delivered Order Cancelled has its own status for a reason. An order cancelled before dispatch costs a phone call. One cancelled after delivery costs the delivery, the product's journey back, and often the product. They are different failures and a client who lumps them together will misjudge where the money is going.

Ownership changes with status, and that is the teaching point. Up to Confirmed the order belongs to the closer. From Assigned through Delivery In Progress it belongs to dispatch and the agent. Coaching a closer on statuses they do not own is the commonest management error this product enables, and chapter two of module four is the report where it shows up.

DRILL: A client asks you to add a status called "Pending Payment". What do you ask first? — Who owns an order in that state, what moves it out, and whether it is terminal. A status without an owner and an exit becomes a place orders go to be forgotten, and the follow-up pool will not rescue them if it is marked terminal.

Why the not-terminal rule matters more than the status list. A consultant who memorises seventeen statuses can recite them. One who understands that non-terminal means "still being chased" can predict what the system will do to any order in front of them, including ones added after they learned the list.

The statuses that describe the customer rather than the order. Not Picking, Not Reachable, Call Back — these record a failure to make contact, not a stage of fulfilment. Grouped with the fulfilment statuses in a chart they distort it; read as a group of their own they are a contactability report, and often the most actionable thing on the dashboard.

lessons.html:
Click any row and a drawer opens from the right with the list still live behind it. Click another row to switch orders; close with the X.

The header carries the order ID — a readable code combining the company and a sequence, such as Daggo Company-CRM-ORD-08-000024 — the customer name, and a Copy details button. Beneath it the status chips lay out the journey travelled: Assigned → Agent Notified → Order Accepted → Delivered. That strip is the fastest read on the screen.

The field block: Status · Order Date & Time · Closer · Dispatch Agent · Expected Delivery · Actual Delivery · and Commitment Fee, with a Record Commitment Fee action. Expected against Actual is the pair to read together — whether the promise was kept.

Then five blocks that answer five different questions. Customer — name, email, phone numbers, and a Call customer action. Lead — where it came from: source such as WhatsApp, the originating number, whether a digital marketer was captured, and the origin. Invoice — the linked sales invoice. Delivery — status and delivered date. Address. Items — item, quantity, unit rate, amount, edit and delete per line, an Add Item action, and the order value.

"Digital marketer: Not captured" is a finding, not a blank. It means this order cannot be attributed to an ad buyer, so it will never appear in Marketing ROAS. A client whose ROAS looks thin should be shown how many of their orders carry that line — it is usually the explanation.

DRILL: A client says an order "is not showing in ROAS". Where do you look? — The Lead block. If the digital marketer was not captured, or the origin is phone or WhatsApp rather than a tracked form, the order is correctly excluded. Ad-attributed leads count only tracked campaign forms.

Why Copy details exists. Support conversations happen in WhatsApp and on phone calls, not inside the product. One button that produces a pasteable summary removes a dozen transcription errors a week. Show it to every client; almost nobody finds it alone.

The invoice link is the boundary between CRM and accounts. An order is a sales conversation; an invoice is a financial document with its own lifecycle. Clients ask for them to be the same thing and they should not be — the moment they merge, cancelling an order starts amending accounting records.

checks.q: 'Digital marketer: Not captured' on an order means:
opts: It cannot be attributed to an ad buyer and will not appear in Marketing ROAS
checks.why: Ad-attributed leads count only orders arriving through a tracked campaign form.

checks.why: Everything else describes the order; those two describe the promise.

checks.q: The order and its sales invoice are kept as separate records because:

checks.why: Merging them would mean cancelling an order amends accounting records.

lessons.title: Editing items — recalculation, locks, and delivery-fee care
lessons.html:
The Items block is the only part of an order that changes money, so it carries the most care.

The mechanics. Add Item opens a picker; choose the item, set quantity, and the unit rate fills from the product with the line amount computed beside it. Each line can be edited or deleted, and the order value recalculates immediately.

Recalculation is instant and total. There is no draft state to review before committing — change a quantity and the order value has changed. Teach closers to confirm the new total aloud to the customer before ending the call, because the system will not prompt them and the customer will remember the first figure.

Where editing gets dangerous is after dispatch. An order whose value changes once an agent is carrying it creates a mismatch between what the customer was told, what the agent expects to collect, and what the invoice says. The discipline is simple and worth stating as a rule: if the order has left, do not edit the items — cancel and re-raise, or record the difference deliberately. The system will let you; that is not the same as it being safe.

Cash on delivery makes this sharper. The agent collects a figure. If it was edited after they set out, the agent and the customer will disagree at the door and the agent will lose. Every value change after dispatch needs a call to whoever is carrying it.

The invoice is linked, not merged. Editing items changes the order; whether and how that flows to a submitted invoice is an accounts question with its own rules. Never assume an edited order silently corrects a submitted invoice.

DRILL: A customer adds an item while the agent is en route, COD. What do you tell the closer to do? — Edit the order, then call the agent with the new total before they arrive. The edit is the easy half; the call is the half that stops an argument at the door.

Why there is no confirmation step on recalculation. Speed. This is a call-centre product and a modal between every quantity change would cost more in aggregate than the errors it prevents. The trade is deliberate, and the mitigation is the habit — say the total aloud — rather than the interface.

The audit question a client eventually asks. "Who changed this value?" Point them at the order's own history rather than reconstructing from the invoice. Establishing that habit early prevents the version of this conversation that happens after money has gone missing.

checks.q: Editing an item's quantity on an order:
opts: Recalculates the order value immediately, with no draft state
checks.why: There is no confirmation step, which is why the habit of confirming the total aloud matters.

checks.q: An order is edited after dispatch on a COD delivery. The essential extra step is:
opts: Call the agent with the new total before they arrive
checks.why: Otherwise the agent and the customer disagree at the door and the agent loses.

checks.q: An edited order and a submitted invoice:
opts: Do not silently reconcile — the invoice follows accounting rules
checks.why: The link is a reference, not a merge.

lessons.title: Assignment, the follow-up pool, and after-sales
lessons.html:
Three mechanisms decide who is working an order and when it comes back. A consultant configures all three, and clients confuse them constantly.

Assignment. Orders reach a closer automatically or by hand. Automatic assignment respects shift management when it is on — only on-shift or always-available closers receive auto-assigned leads — and manual assignment by a manager is never blocked. In the drawer, Closer and Dispatch Agent are separate fields because they are separate jobs: one sold it, one is carrying it.

The follow-up pool catches stalled orders. Orders not in a terminal status enter the pool automatically after a configured number of days from creation — the threshold is a setting, and the product's own default is ten. The pool itself is a workspace: filters across pool, status, country, brand and branch, columns for order, customer, category, status, phone, value, sent-on and claimed-by, and three actions — Claim, Release, Convert.

Claim is a lock, and that is the point. An unclaimed order shows "unclaimed" and anyone may take it; a claimed one shows who holds it. Two people cannot ring the same customer an hour apart, which is the failure the pool exists to prevent. Release puts it back rather than abandoning it.

After-sales is the opposite motion: not chasing a stalled order but returning to a completed one. When enabled, delivered orders schedule a reorder chase on a computed date — fourteen days for a single-unit order, twenty-nine for multi-unit, the latter chosen so the call lands one or two days before a thirty-day supply runs out. The workspace shows active cases, contacted, completed and escalated, with tabs for My Cases, Team, Unassigned, Scheduled and Done.

"Unassigned" in after-sales is explained on screen: manual bucket — no eligible closer was available at sweep time. It is a coverage finding, not a person's backlog.

DRILL: A client sets the follow-up threshold to one day, and the pool fills with thousands of orders. What has gone wrong? — Nothing technical. A one-day threshold means every order not terminal by tomorrow is "stalled", which is most of them. The threshold should sit just beyond a normal fulfilment cycle; inside it, the pool stops meaning anything.

Why the reorder cadence is a number worth defending. Twenty-nine days is not arbitrary — it is thirty minus the lead time to redeliver. A client who moves it to thirty-five has decided their customers should run out before being asked. Explain the reasoning and they usually leave it alone.

Backfill lookback exists to protect closers. When the backfill runs, only delivered orders within the lookback are considered, so switching after-sales on for an established client does not bury the team under two years of historical cases.

opts: Not in a terminal status after the configured number of days from creation
Older than 30 days regardless of status
checks.why: Terminal orders — Delivered, Cancelled, Duplicate, Rescheduled — are finished and excluded.

It is one month minus a day

lessons.title: Customers — directory, quick actions, and tag discipline
lessons.html:
The customer directory is the other axis on the same data: orders answer "what is happening", customers answer "who is this". It is role-scoped like orders.

What a customer record carries: identity — name, phone, email — and history: their orders, what they have spent, when they last bought, and where they came from. The timeline is the part consultants underuse. Before any conversation with a customer, it is the difference between "how can I help" and "I see the Baozem order was rescheduled twice — let me sort that".

Phone is the identity field. It is what the duplicate check uses, what after-sales dials, and what a customer gives on a call. Email is frequently absent and never a reliable key. Any client planning a data migration should be told this before they map their columns, not after.

Repeat Customer is a channel in Attribution, and this is where that number comes from. A customer record with several orders is the asset the business built; the directory is where you can see whether there are many of them or a few. A client whose directory is mostly single-order records is buying every sale, however good this month looks.

Tag discipline, since tags are free text and free text rots. Three rules: agree the vocabulary before anyone types, keep it short enough to remember, and review it quarterly. Fuel, fuel and Petrol are three tags to a database and one idea to a human. Consultants who set this up on day one save clients a cleanup that otherwise never happens.

DRILL: A client wants to tag customers by twelve behavioural segments. What do you advise? — Start with three or four they will actually use. Twelve tags means inconsistent tagging within a month, and inconsistent tags are worse than none because they look like data. Add more when the first four are being used correctly.

Why the customer directory is the right screen for a retention conversation and cohorts is the right screen for a retention decision. The directory shows individuals and is persuasive; cohorts show the pattern and are correct. Use the first to make a client care and the second to work out what to do.

The migration trap. Clients arriving with spreadsheets have customers keyed on name or email. Both produce duplicates on arrival — two Felix Akhigbes, one customer with three email addresses. Key on phone, deduplicate before import, and accept that some records will need a human. Doing it afterwards costs several times more.

c3.title: ZhiftCRM Consultant — The Campaign Engine: Forms, Submissions & Carts
c3.desc: The campaign engine: lead forms end to end, the three builder steps with package pricing and the routing that product category decides, publishing and the token, embedding by iframe or WordPress plugin including the CORS decision, and the two lists — submissions and abandoned carts — with the recovery discipline that turns the second into revenue.

lessons.title: Lead forms — what they are, end to end
lessons.html:
A lead form is a hosted page where a customer chooses a product, enters their details and places an order without speaking to anyone first. It replaces the old funnel — advertisement, phone number, agent, manual order — with a page that creates the order itself.

The whole path, so you can hold it in one sentence: a media buyer builds a form, publishes it, embeds it on a landing page or Facebook tab, the ad sends traffic to it, a submission arrives, and it becomes an order attributed to that buyer and that campaign. Every report in module four downstream of "ad-attributed" depends on this chain being intact.

Campaigns → Lead Forms lists them: form name with its token beneath (or DRAFT), default item, digital marketer, status — Published or Draft — lead count, and last submission. Actions per row: Duplicate, Edit, Details.

Each media buyer sees only the forms they created. That is a visibility rule, not a permission fault, and it is the first thing to say when a buyer reports that forms are missing. An administrator sees all of them.

Duplicate is the most useful button on the screen. A working form is a tested configuration — category, packages, fields, appearance. Duplicating it for a new campaign preserves everything that was got right and changes only what needs to change. Teach it early or clients rebuild from scratch each time and introduce a new mistake every time.

DRILL: A media buyer says their leads stopped arriving overnight and nothing was changed. What do you check on this screen? — The form's status. A form reverted to Draft is unpublished and its embed stops producing submissions, while the page it sits on continues to look perfectly normal.

Why the form list is also a performance report. Lead count and last submission sit on every row. A form with hundreds of leads and a last submission three weeks old is either a campaign that ended or an embed that broke, and this screen is where the difference is visible earliest — well before anyone notices in ROAS.

The draft that never shipped. Forms accumulate. A client with a hundred and fifty-nine of them has perhaps a dozen live, and the rest are experiments. That is fine, but it makes the list unnavigable, so agree a naming convention on day one: campaign, country, product. Nobody ever does this retrospectively.

checks.q: A media buyer cannot see forms a colleague created. This is:
opts: The visibility rule — each buyer sees only their own forms
checks.why: Administrators see all forms; buyers see their own by design.

checks.q: Leads stop arriving from a form that was working. Check first:
opts: Whether the form is still Published rather than Draft
checks.why: An unpublished form stops producing submissions while the page still looks normal.

checks.q: Duplicating an existing form for a new campaign is preferred because:
opts: It preserves a tested configuration and changes only what must change
checks.why: Rebuilding from scratch introduces a fresh mistake each time.

lessons.title: Step 1: Basics — every field, and why each converts
lessons.html:
The builder is three steps — Basics, Builder, Upsell — and you can move between them freely, with a Save draft at any point and a Resume draft picker to come back later.

Form title is internal: it names the form in the list and in reports. Name it so a stranger can find it — campaign, product, country.

Digital marketer is the attribution field, and it is the most consequential box on the page. It decides who this form's leads are credited to in Marketing ROAS. Set it wrong and the buyer's numbers are wrong for the life of the campaign.

Redirect URL sends the customer somewhere after submitting — a thank-you page, usually, and the place a conversion pixel fires. Success message is what they see if you do not redirect. Use one or the other deliberately rather than leaving both at defaults.

Submit button text is a conversion lever and costs nothing to test. Quantity display mode — radio buttons, for instance — changes how the customer chooses how many, and radio buttons make the intended quantity visible rather than leaving a number field at one.

Preset country is the field with a hidden consequence, stated plainly on screen: if set, buyers won't see the country field and state/city will use this country. For a single-market campaign that is one fewer field and a better conversion rate. For a multi-country campaign it silently misfiles every order.

DRILL: A client running Nigeria and Ghana from one form reports that Ghanaian orders show as Nigeria. What happened? — Preset country is set. It hides the field and forces the value. One form per country, or no preset — those are the only two correct answers.

Why every removed field raises conversion and lowers data quality. Each box is a chance to abandon and a fact you wanted. Preset country is free — the customer gains, you lose nothing, because you knew the country already. Removing address line 2 is a trade. Removing phone is not a trade at all; it is removing the only reliable identity field the system has.

The attribution field deserves a checklist entry. It is a dropdown, it defaults to somebody, and nobody notices it at publish time. Six weeks later a buyer's ROAS is inexplicable and the cause is one unchanged dropdown.

opts: Hides the country field and forces state and city to that country
Sets a default the customer can change
Restricts which closers receive the leads
checks.why: Excellent for a single-market campaign, silently wrong for a multi-country one.

checks.q: The Digital Marketer field on a form decides:
opts: Who the leads are credited to in Marketing ROAS
checks.why: Set wrong, it makes that buyer's return figures wrong for the life of the campaign.

checks.q: Removing the phone field from a form is:
opts: Removing the only reliable identity field the system has
checks.why: Phone drives the duplicate check, after-sales dialling and customer matching.

lessons.title: Step 2: Builder — routing, products, packages, fields
lessons.html:
Step 2 does four jobs, and the first is structural.

Order dimensions. Choose one Product Category — it is required — and Resolved Brand and Resolved Cost Center fill automatically and are read-only. The category is not a label; it is the routing decision. It determines the brand the order belongs to, the cost centre it books against, and which closers are eligible to receive it, because remit is set by category. Choose it wrong and the order goes to the wrong people and the wrong ledger.

Core field options. Every built-in field carries two independent toggles, Required and Visible: Full Name, Email, Phone, Address Line 1, Address Line 2, Country, State/Province, City, Postal Code. Two toggles rather than one is deliberate — a field can be visible and optional, which is how you ask for an email without losing the customers who will not give one.

Offer packages, and here is the mechanism people get wrong. A package carries a label, a buy quantity, a free quantity, a fixed package amount and a discount amount, with one marked default. The fixed amount is the price of the whole package, not a multiple of the unit price. "Buy 1" at 18,500 and "Buy 2" at 30,000 is a bundle at 15,000 each — the saving is the offer. Enter 37,000 for the two-pack and you have built a package with no reason to exist.

Linked items are the actual products behind it, with type, quantity, price and a default. Additional questions add custom fields — pickup store, delivery instructions, financing — on top of the core order fields rather than instead of them.

DRILL: A client's two-pack sells nothing while the single sells well. First thing to check? — The fixed package amount. If the two-pack is priced at exactly twice the single, there is no offer, and customers are correctly declining to buy two of something at no saving.

Why packages beat quantity fields. A quantity box asks the customer to do arithmetic and decide. A package makes the decision for them and shows the saving. The same order value arrives more often — which is the whole of offer design, and it lives in five fields on this screen.

Free quantity is the other lever, and it reads differently. Buy two get one free is the same money as a third off three, and converts differently in different markets. It costs nothing to run both as separate forms and let the numbers decide — which is what Duplicate is for.

checks.q: The Fixed Package Amount on an offer package is:
opts: The price of the whole package, not a multiple of the unit price
The per-unit price within the package
checks.why: Buy 2 at 30,000 against Buy 1 at 18,500 is a bundle at 15,000 each; the saving is the offer.

checks.q: Product Category on a form is structural because it determines:
opts: Brand, cost centre and which closers are eligible to receive the order
Only how the form is labelled
checks.why: Brand and cost centre resolve from it automatically, and closer remit is set by category.

checks.q: Core fields carry both Required and Visible toggles so that:
opts: A field can be shown but optional
checks.why: It is how you ask for an email without losing customers who will not give one.

lessons.title: Appearance, upsell, publish — and what publishing produces
lessons.html:
Appearance sits beside the builder: button background and text colour, page and card background, heading colour, input border colour and radius, and font family. Open live preview opens a separate tab showing the theme as you edit.

The trust principle beats the brand guideline. A form that looks like the page it is embedded in converts better than one that looks like software. Match the client's landing page, not their logo palette — the customer never saw the brand book and is deciding, in about a second, whether this page is real.

Step 3 is a single upsell, shown after submit. The product says so: configure the single post-submit offer shown on step 3. One offer. The fields are the offer itself plus its persuasion: upsell item, a product-details URL, an optional logo, heading, description, form width, text colour, button text, decline text and optional scarcity text.

The decline text is not a formality. "No, I don't want this additional offer" is a real sentence a real person reads, and writing it graciously rather than manipulatively is the difference between a customer who declines and completes and one who abandons a purchase they had already made.

Publish produces two artefacts, and the token is the important one. The Details panel shows the token, status, default item, leads and last submission, plus an iframe snippet pointing at the hosted form with the token in the query string. Buttons: Edit form, Preview, Copy URL, Copy embed, Open form.

The token identifies the form everywhere — in the iframe, in the WordPress shortcode, in support conversations. When a client reports a problem with "the liver form", ask for the token. There are usually three forms with similar names and only one of them is live.

DRILL: A client's embedded form shows an old price. They swear they updated it. What is the likeliest cause? — They edited a different form. Ask for the token in the embed on the live page and compare it with the token of the form they edited. Duplicated forms with similar names are the usual explanation.

Why the upsell is limited to one. Two consecutive upsells convert the second far worse and cost goodwill on an order already won. The constraint is a design opinion, and a good one — a client asking for a chain of three is asking to spend a completed sale on a maybe.

Scarcity text, and the line not to cross. Optional limited-time copy raises conversion. Copy that is untrue — a countdown that resets, a stock figure that is invented — raises conversion once and costs the customer permanently. Advise clients to use it only where it is true.

checks.why: Consecutive upsells convert worse and risk goodwill on an order already won.

checks.q: When a client reports a problem with a form, ask for:
checks.why: Names are duplicated; the token identifies the form in the embed, the shortcode and support.

checks.q: Form appearance should be matched to:
opts: The landing page it is embedded in
checks.why: A form that looks like the page around it reads as real; one that looks like software does not.

lessons.title: Embedding — iframe, WordPress plugin, and the CORS decision
lessons.html:
A published form has to reach a customer, and there are two routes. This chapter is where consultants actually get called.

The iframe is universal. Copy embed gives a snippet pointing at the hosted form with the token in the query string, sized to full width with a maximum and a fixed height. It works on any page that accepts HTML — a Facebook tab, a microsite, a landing page builder. It is the fallback that always works.

The WordPress plugin is the better route for WordPress clients, because the form renders in the page rather than inside a frame. Install it from the WordPress admin by upload, or by FTP if the client's host forbids uploads. Then the shortcode:

[pangea_form token="your_token_here"]

Three attributes. token is required. theme takes auto, inherit or minimal — inherit makes the form adopt the site's own styling, which is the trust principle again. class adds a CSS class for anything bespoke. There is a Gutenberg block and Elementor support for clients who do not paste shortcodes.

The decision that needs you: Proxy Mode. By default submissions go straight from the visitor's browser to the CRM, which requires CORS to be configured on the CRM. Where that cannot be done, enable Proxy API Calls in the plugin settings and submissions route through the client's WordPress server instead — WordPress to CRM. No CORS at all, at the cost of two hops instead of one and a little latency.

Diagnose it by the symptom. A form that renders perfectly and fails silently on submit is the classic CORS signature. Before rebuilding anything, turn on proxy mode and try again — it takes a minute and resolves it or rules it out.

DRILL: A client's form displays correctly but nothing arrives in Submissions. Where do you start? — Not with the form. Submit a test through the hosted URL directly: if that works, the form is fine and the problem is the embed — CORS, and proxy mode is the fix. If the hosted URL also fails, the problem is the form.

Why the hosted URL is the diagnostic tool. It removes the client's site from the equation entirely. Every embedding problem divides into "the form is broken" and "the page hosting it is broken", and one test tells you which half you are in. Consultants who skip it debug both halves at once.

Multiple forms on one page. Supported, and worth knowing before a client asks — a comparison page with a form per product is a legitimate design. Each needs its own token, which is another reason for a naming convention that survives contact with a real campaign.

lessons.title: Submissions and abandoned carts — what each list is telling you
lessons.html:
Two lists sit under Campaigns beside Lead Forms, and they answer opposite questions: who finished, and who did not.

Submissions are completed forms. The list runs newest first with summary cards above it and a timespan control, and the action that matters is convert — a submission becomes an order, attributed to the form and therefore to the media buyer who owns it. A submission that is never converted is a customer who filled in your form and was ignored.

Abandoned carts are the other half: customers who started but did not complete their order. Interaction starts the tracking — a product chosen, details being typed — so a page view alone creates nothing. The columns are contact (name, phone, email), items, campaign, when it was abandoned, resumes, and a Convert action.

Resumes is the most underused number in the product. It counts how many times that person came back to the form. A cart with three resumes is somebody who returned twice and still did not finish — that is not a cold lead, it is a person with an unresolved objection, and they are worth calling before a fresh lead is.

The scale is the point. A working installation shows tens of thousands of abandoned carts against a much smaller number of submissions. That ratio is not a failure; it is normal for public forms, and it means the recovery list is a permanent standing asset rather than a queue to be cleared. Teach clients to work it by priority, forever, rather than to try to empty it.

DRILL: A client asks whether they should reduce form fields because their abandoned cart count is enormous. Your answer? — Look at where abandonment happens before removing anything. A large count is expected. Removing phone to reduce it would cost you the only field that makes recovery possible, and recovery is worth more than the abandonment you prevented.

Why abandoned carts are a better lead source than most paid traffic. The person chose a product and began giving you their details. They are further down the funnel than anyone an advertisement will reach today, and they cost nothing to contact. A client spending on cold traffic while ignoring a cart list is buying what they already have.

The priority order worth writing on the wall: recent and high value with a phone number first; then anything with multiple resumes; then the rest by freshness. Beyond a few days the return collapses, so a cart list worked weekly is worth a fraction of one worked daily.

lessons.title: Cart recovery — prioritisation, outreach, conversion
lessons.html:
Recovery is a discipline, not a task, and it lives or dies on the order in which the list is worked.

The priority order. First: high value, phone present, abandoned within about two hours — call these before anything else, including fresh leads. Second: any value, phone present, within twenty-four hours. Third: multiple resumes at any age, because repeated return means real intent. Last: everything else, by freshness.

Speed dominates every other factor. The same cart converts dramatically better at two hours than at two days, and by a week it is close to a cold call. If a client can only do one thing with this list, it is to work the top of it today rather than all of it eventually.

What to say, and what not to. The customer chose a product and stopped; they know they did. Opening with "I saw you didn't complete your order" is accurate and slightly accusatory. Opening with the product — "I'm calling about the Baozem order, I can complete it for you now" — treats it as an order in progress, which is what it is.

The three real objections behind most abandonment: price, trust, and a practical obstacle — delivery time, payment method, an address they were unsure about. The last is the most common and the easiest to solve, and you only find it by asking. Nobody abandons a form because the button was the wrong colour.

Convert closes the loop. The cart becomes an order attributed to the same form and campaign, so recovered revenue lands in the right place in ROAS. A client recovering carts and raising the orders manually is losing the attribution and will under-report their own campaigns.

DRILL: A client assigns cart recovery to whoever is free. What do you recommend instead? — Name someone. A list worked by whoever has a spare moment is worked at the wrong end and never twice by the same person, so nobody learns which objections recur. One owner working the top daily beats five people working it occasionally.

Why recovery belongs to a closer rather than to marketing. It is a sales conversation with an objection to handle, not a message to send. Clients often route it to whoever runs campaigns, because the cart came from a form. Attribution belongs to the form; the phone call belongs to somebody who sells.

The number to report to a client, monthly. Recovered revenue as a share of abandoned value, and the median age at recovery. The first proves the discipline is worth funding; the second shows whether it is being worked daily or in bursts.

c4.title: ZhiftCRM Consultant — Reports & the Numbers
c4.desc: The report library at consultant level: who each report belongs to and how scope follows reporting tier, the two rates on Closer Performance and what each failure means, fairness when comparing closers, ROAS against the client's own profitability threshold, the mix and channel reads, and cohorts as the test of whether anything is being built.

lessons.title: The report directory — categories, roles, and the universal date filter
lessons.html:
Nineteen reports sit under Reports, and a consultant's first question is never "what does this report say" but "who is this report for". Show a closer the cluster view and you have handed them their colleagues' numbers; show a cluster lead only their own summary and you have hidden the job from them.

ReportWhose screen
My Summarythe closer — their own orders, nobody else's
Orders Status (Overview / Closer Performance)closer managers
Team Closer Summaryteam leads — their team, and themselves in it
Cluster Members Statuscluster leads
Digital Marketer Leads · Ad Buyer Categories · Marketing ROASmedia buyers (also called digital marketers, also called ad buyers — three names, one role)
Upsell / Cross-sellclosers
Product Sales · Attribution · Cohort Trends · Branch Performancethe business — owner, manager, you

Scope is not a filter you apply; it is applied to you. Cluster Members Status states it outright: scope follows your reporting tier automatically. The same URL shows a cluster lead their cluster and a manager the lot. When a client says "the report is wrong, I can't see Lagos", the first check is their tier, not the data.

The date control is not one control. Most reports carry a period selector — Daily, Monthly, Custom — and several carry a second field, Date Type, which decides which date is being filtered: order date, delivery date, and so on. Two reports over "August" disagree constantly and almost always because one counted when the order arrived and the other when it landed. Establish the date type before you debug the numbers.

DRILL: A team lead says their delivery rate is 45% but the manager's screen shows 58% for the same week. Where do you look first? — Not at the data. At scope and date type: the lead sees their team, the manager sees everyone, and one of the two screens may be filtering on delivery date rather than order date. Reconcile the question before reconciling the figures.

Why the role mapping matters more than the feature list. Every report here is technically available to explain, and a demonstration that walks all nineteen teaches nothing. What a client remembers is this is your screen, that one is your manager's. Deployments fail on people not knowing which number they are accountable for, far more often than on a report being wrong.

The reports that answer the same question differently. Orders Status, Team Closer Summary and Cluster Members Status all count orders by closer. They are not redundant — they differ in scope and in what they let you do next. Knowing why three exist is the difference between configuring a client's reporting and listing it.

opts: My Summary is scoped to the person viewing it; a manager's view exists and is a different report
A permission is missing and should be granted
The report is broken and needs a refresh
They should use Cluster Members Status instead
checks.why: Scope follows reporting tier by design, not by configuration error.

opts: Which date type each is filtering on, and each viewer's scope
Which report was opened most recently
checks.why: Order date versus delivery date, and tier scope, explain most disagreements before any data is at fault.

opts: Three names for the same role
Three separate roles with different permissions
checks.why: One role, three labels — worth saying plainly to a client before it confuses a training session.

lessons.title: Closer Summary — every column, the red flags, the coaching reads
lessons.html:
Orders Status carries six cards and two tabs. The cards: Total Orders · Total Value · Pending · Delivered · Confirmation Rate · Delivery Rate. The tabs: Overview, and Closer Performance, which is the coaching screen.

Closer Performance lists, per closer: Total Orders · Confirmed · Delivered · Value · Confirmation Rate. Two rates, and they fail for different reasons — this is the whole of the chapter.

PatternWhat it meansCoaching read
Low confirmation, delivery fine on what confirmslosing the customer on the calla closer problem — script, objection handling, speed to first call
Confirmation good, delivery poorthe customer said yes and the order died afterrarely the closer — dispatch, stock, address quality, agent coverage
Both low, volume highquantity without qualitycheck lead source before blaming anyone
Both 100%, volume 1nothing at alla single order proves nothing; say so rather than praising it

"Unassigned" appears as a row in the closer list. It is not a person. It is orders nobody owns, and it carries a value like any other row — four orders worth ₦77,000 in the screen this chapter was written from. That row is a finding, not a closer: it means leads arrived while no one was on shift, or auto-assignment had nobody eligible. Never coach it; escalate it.

The denominator discipline. Confirmation Rate is colour-coded, and a red 0.0% on three orders and a red 0.0% on ninety are entirely different facts. The colour treats them identically. Read the volume column first, every time, or you will performance-manage somebody for a bad Tuesday.

DRILL: A closer shows 2 orders, 2 confirmed, 2 delivered, 100%. The client wants them made team lead. Your answer? — On two orders you know nothing. Ask for the same view over a quarter. A rate without a denominator is a rumour, and promoting on one is how a client stops trusting the reports.

Why confirmation and delivery must never be averaged into one "performance" number. A client will ask for it — a single score, sortable. It would merge a problem the closer owns with one they do not, and the person at the bottom would be whoever happened to sell into a region with poor dispatch. Refuse it and explain why; that refusal is most of what they are paying you for.

The conversation this report actually starts. Not "who is worst" but "why does this row look like that". Closers know things the report cannot — a product out of stock, a brand the market has turned on. The report tells you where to ask; it does not tell you the answer.

checks.q: A closer's confirmation rate is high but delivery rate is poor. The likeliest cause is:
opts: Something after the sale — dispatch, stock, address quality
checks.why: Confirmation is the closer's; what happens after the yes usually is not.

checks.q: 'Unassigned' shows in the Closer Performance list with four orders. It should be treated as:
opts: A finding to escalate — orders nobody owns
A closer with a poor record
checks.why: It means auto-assignment found nobody eligible, or leads arrived with no coverage.

checks.q: Before reading any rate on this report you should first read:
checks.why: A rate on two orders and a rate on two hundred are coloured the same and mean nothing alike.

lessons.title: Team Performance — aggregates and the fairness metric
lessons.html:
Team Closer Summary is the team lead's screen — their team, and themselves inside it. Cards: Total Orders · Delivered · Delivery Rate · Cancelled · Rejected · Delivered Value. Filters run wide: period, state, marketer, brand, category, branch, country.

Two panels do the work. Closers in Scope — closer, team manager, orders, delivered, delivery %, cancelled. And Top Delivery Rates, a bar chart, green for good and red for poor, on a fixed 0–100 axis.

That fixed axis is the fairness problem in one picture. A closer with one order and one delivery draws a full green bar identical to a closer with forty of forty. The chart is honest about rate and silent about weight. Read it beside the Orders column or do not read it at all.

The fairness metric, stated plainly: compare rates only within comparable volume, and compare volume only within comparable opportunity. A closer working a strong brand in a well-covered branch is not being compared like-for-like with one working a thin category in a region where dispatch is weak. The filters exist so you can hold those things still — filter to one brand, one branch, then compare.

Cluster Members Status is the tier above: one row per cluster member, one column per order status — New Lead, Qualified, Confirmed, Assigned, Agent Notified, Dispatch Assigned, Order Accepted, Processing, Delivery In Progress, Delivered, Delivered Order Cancelled, Failed, Cancelled, Returned, Rejected, Duplicate, On Hold — and a Totals row. It answers a different question: not how good is this person but where is the work stuck. A column that is heavy across every member is a process fault, not a people fault.

DRILL: Top Delivery Rates shows nine closers at 100% and one at 50%, and the client wants the 50% one managed out. What do you say? — Ask for the Orders column. If the nine are on one order each and the tenth is on twenty, the tenth is the only person you have any evidence about, and they are probably your best closer.

Reading a status column rather than a person row. The cluster matrix is usually taught row-wise, because rows are people and people are what managers ask about. Read it column-wise and it becomes an operations report: a stack in Agent Notified across ten members means agents are not responding; a stack in Assigned means closers are not calling. Neither shows up row by row.

Where "Delivered Order Cancelled" sits. It has its own column for a reason — an order that was delivered and then cancelled is a different failure from one cancelled before dispatch, and it costs the business the delivery. When that column is non-zero, the conversation is about returns and refusals, not selling.

checks.q: The Top Delivery Rates chart plots every closer on a 0–100 axis. Its main limitation is:
opts: It shows rate without weight — one order can draw a full bar
It only shows the top three
checks.why: Rate is meaningless without the order count beside it.

checks.q: A single status column is heavy across every cluster member. That indicates:
opts: A process fault at that stage
A training need for one person
checks.why: What is common to everyone is not about any of them.

checks.q: Comparing two closers fairly on this report requires:
opts: Holding brand, branch and period still, then comparing within similar volume
Using the widest date range available
checks.why: Opportunity differs by brand, branch and period; the filters exist to remove that difference.

lessons.title: ROAS — the formula, the profitability threshold, the budget loop
lessons.html:
Marketing ROAS is the budget report, and the most misread screen in the product. Cards: Total Spend · Ad-Attributed Leads · Delivered Orders · Delivered Revenue · Delivery Rate · ROAS · ROI. Tabs: By Campaign · By Order · By Product · By Marketer · Spend Entries. Filters: period, from, to, campaign, country, brand — plus a Log Ad Spend button, which matters more than it looks.

ROAS and ROI are the same arithmetic said two ways, and clients confuse them. On one real period: spend ₦256,549,638, delivered revenue ₦714,888,736 — ROAS 2.79x and ROI 178.7%. ROAS is revenue ÷ spend. ROI is the gain over spend, so it is always ROAS minus one, expressed as a percentage. Neither is profit.

The theorem to carry into every client conversation: ROAS measures revenue, not profit. Profitability needs ROAS greater than 1 ÷ gross margin. At 50% margins the threshold is 2.0 — a campaign at 2.0 broke even. At 30% margins it is 3.33. Compute the client's own threshold in the first reporting session and write it on the report, because without it every number here flatters.

The attribution caveat, which the product states and consultants skip. Ad-Attributed Leads counts only leads that arrived through a tracked campaign form, credited to an ad buyer. It excludes phone, WhatsApp and manually entered orders, so it is lower than Total Leads Generated on the Digital Marketer Leads tab. The two figures are both right and will never match. Say that before a client finds it themselves.

Spend Entries is where the report is true or false. Spend is logged by hand — date, campaign, country, amount, owner, notes — and every ROAS on the screen inherits whatever was typed. A campaign with spend missing shows a spectacular ROAS. Check the entries before you interpret the ratios; a 10.14x that nobody can explain is usually an unlogged invoice, not a genius.

DRILL: A client sees ROAS 2.4x and wants to triple the budget. Their gross margin is 35%. Your answer? — Their threshold is 1 ÷ 0.35 = 2.86. At 2.4 they are losing money on that campaign. Tripling it triples the loss. Fix targeting and creative first, and if it has not crossed 2.86 in two weeks, cut it.

The budget loop, in order. Sort by ROAS descending. Identify the top three to five and consider raising their budgets. Identify everything under the client's own profitability threshold. Optimise those first — targeting, creative, offer — and if ROAS has not moved within two weeks, reduce or pause. Re-run monthly. The loop only works if the threshold was computed from the client's margin rather than borrowed from an article.

Why By Marketer is the tab that starts arguments. It ranks people by spend, delivered value, delivered % and ROAS. A buyer with a small budget and a narrow product will out-ROAS one carrying the flagship spend, every time. Rank within comparable budget or the report becomes a weapon rather than an instrument.

checks.q: A client's gross margin is 40%. Their ROAS profitability threshold is:
checks.why: 1 ÷ 0.40 = 2.5. Below that, revenue does not cover the cost of goods plus the ad spend.

checks.q: Ad-Attributed Leads is lower than Total Leads Generated because it:
opts: Excludes phone, WhatsApp and manually entered orders
checks.why: Only leads through a tracked campaign form are credited to an ad buyer.

checks.q: One campaign shows ROAS 10.14x, far above every other. Check first:
opts: Whether all its ad spend has been logged in Spend Entries
Whether to double its budget immediately
checks.why: Spend is entered by hand; missing spend produces a spectacular and false ratio.

lessons.title: Product Sales & Channel Attribution — mix, pricing signals, channel truth
lessons.html:
Product Sales answers what is selling. Cards: Total Units Sold · Total Sales Amount · Unique SKUs Sold · Top Product. The distribution chart carries a toggle — By Sales or By Units — and that toggle is the chapter.

A product's share of units and its share of naira are different numbers, and the gap between them is a pricing signal. On one real period a product held 12.5% of units and 7% of sales; another held 0.7% of units and 14.4% of sales. The first moves volume at a low price, the second is a high-value item selling rarely. Neither fact is visible with the toggle in one position, which is why clients who only ever look at one of them make the wrong call about which line to push.

The Product Performance table gives product group, SKU, product name, units sold, sales value, units % and sales % — the two percentages side by side, so you can read the divergence without toggling at all.

Attribution answers where revenue comes from. Revenue by Channel, with channel, revenue, orders, average order and share, over the usual timeframe control. The channels are real routes, not campaigns: WhatsApp, Repeat Customer, WordPress, Phone.

Repeat Customer is a channel, and that is the most useful thing on the screen. It separates revenue you paid to acquire from revenue you already earned. A client celebrating strong revenue while their non-repeat channels shrink is watching their own base carry them, and that is a finite trick. The average order column is the second read: a channel with fewer orders but a far higher average is worth more attention than its share suggests.

DRILL: Attribution shows WhatsApp at 54.3% of revenue on 11 orders; Repeat Customer at 35.3% on 13. The client wants to cut WhatsApp spend because it has fewer orders. Your answer? — WhatsApp's average order is ₦51,591 against ₦28,346. Fewer orders, larger ones. Cutting it removes the most valuable route, and Repeat Customer is not a route you can buy more of.

Why Attribution and ROAS will not reconcile, and should not. Attribution counts revenue by the channel it arrived through, all of it. ROAS counts only what a tracked campaign form attributed to an ad buyer, and excludes phone, WhatsApp and manual orders entirely. A client comparing the two and finding a gap has found the design, not a fault. Explain it once, early, in writing.

Unique SKUs Sold, the quiet number. It counts breadth. A month where units and revenue held steady but unique SKUs fell means the range is narrowing — fewer lines carrying the same weight. That is a concentration risk long before it is a revenue problem, and nothing else on the dashboard shows it.

checks.q: A product holds 0.7% of units and 14.4% of sales value. It is:
opts: A high-value item selling in low volume
checks.why: The gap between unit share and value share is the pricing signal.

checks.q: 'Repeat Customer' appearing as a channel in Attribution lets you:
opts: Separate revenue you paid to acquire from revenue the existing base produced
checks.why: A business carried by its own base is not growing, however good the revenue looks.

checks.q: Attribution revenue and ROAS delivered revenue do not match. This is:
opts: Expected — ROAS counts only ad-attributed orders
checks.why: Attribution counts every channel; ROAS counts only tracked campaign forms.

lessons.title: Revenue Cohorts — the matrix, healthy retention, warning signs
lessons.html:
Cohort Trends groups customers by when they first bought and tracks what each group spends in the months after. It is the only report here that answers whether the business is building anything, as opposed to selling something.

Read it as a matrix: a row per cohort — the month they first bought — and a column per month since. The first column is acquisition. Everything to its right is retention, and retention is the whole point.

What you seeWhat it means
Row falls sharply after month 1, near zero by month 3a one-purchase business — every naira of growth must be bought
Row declines then flattensa genuine repeat base; the flat part is the asset
Recent rows thinner than older rows at the same ageacquisition quality is falling — the newer customers are worth less
A row that rises after month 2usually a reorder cadence landing, not a miracle

That last row is where this report meets the rest of the product. After-sales reorder scheduling puts a chase call on delivered orders at a computed date — fourteen days for a single-unit order, twenty-nine for multi-unit, so the call lands a day or two before a thirty-day supply runs out. A cohort that lifts in month one is often that machinery working. If cohorts are flat and the reorder cadence is switched off, you have found the client's cheapest available growth.

The comparison that matters is same-age, not same-month. Comparing a January cohort's month-six figure against an August cohort's month-one figure tells you nothing except that January had longer. Read down a column, not across a row.

DRILL: A client's revenue is up 30% year on year, but every cohort row flattens near zero by month three. What have you found? — A business buying its growth. Revenue is rising because acquisition is rising, and the day ad spend stops, so does revenue. That is a strategy conversation, not a reporting one, and this is the only screen that shows it.

Why cohorts are the report clients ask for last and need most. Every other screen rewards a good month. This one asks whether last year's good months are still paying, and the answer is frequently uncomfortable. Bring it to a quarterly review rather than a weekly one — it moves too slowly to watch and too meaningfully to skip.

The small-cohort trap. An early month with nine customers will swing wildly and mean almost nothing; a later month with nine hundred will move slowly and mean a great deal. Cohort tables invite eye-reading across a grid where the rows have wildly different weights. Check the cohort size before believing any row, the same discipline as the denominator on Closer Performance.

c5.title: ZhiftCRM Consultant — Administration: Closers & Shifts
c5.desc: Administration at consultant level: the Closer record and the golden rule, the six blocks and why remit decides fairness, the creation sequence and its three recipes, an ordered diagnosis that beats intuition, and shift management from its rules to a rollout that survives its first uncovered hour.

lessons.title: The Closer record — what it is, and the golden rule
lessons.html:
A Closer is the record representing a salesperson who works leads and orders, and almost everything in the product routes through it. Auto-assignment targets closers. Orders attribute to them. The follow-up pool draws from them. Every performance report counts by them.

The golden rule: the Closer must link to a User account, and the link is by email. Get that link wrong and everything downstream behaves strangely without erroring — the person logs in and sees nothing that belongs to them, or leads assign to a name nobody recognises. It is the single highest-value check in the entire administration module, and it takes four seconds.

Two records, one person, and neither creates the other. A User is who logs in. A Closer is who receives work. Creating a User does not create a Closer. The commonest onboarding fault in the product is a real person with a working login and no Closer record: they are present, they are enabled, they are waiting, and auto-assignment cannot see them at all.

What happens when a closer leaves. The instinct is to delete. Do not. Their orders, their history and every report they appear in depend on the record existing. Disable it instead — new assignments stop, history is preserved, and the reports remain truthful about the months they worked. A deleted closer takes their past with them, and the first month-end after that is painful.

DRILL: A client reports a closer "not receiving any leads" on their first morning. What do you check, in order? — Does a Closer record exist at all; is it enabled; does it link to the right User by email; does the person have categories or a remit that matches the leads arriving. In practice the answer is one of the first three about nine times in ten.

Why the golden rule is stated as a rule rather than a step. Steps get skipped when somebody is in a hurry; rules get checked. A consultant who says "confirm the User link by email" at every handover, every time, prevents more support tickets than any amount of training on the rest of the form.

The symptom that never says what it is. Nothing errors when the link is wrong. The person simply has an empty screen and a suspicion that the software is broken, and clients escalate that as a bug. Recognising the shape of it — quiet, plausible, and entirely a configuration fault — is what separates a consultant from a manual.
